channel.title: Acme: Science Fiction and Fantasy News
channel.description: Science fiction and fantasy fandom news, publishing, conventions, and history.

item.title: J. J. Pierce, Galaxy editor and combative New Wave critic, dies at 85
item.description: An obituary published November 10, 2026, reports that John Jeremy Pierce died November 1 at age 85. Pierce edited the fanzine Renaissance in the late 1960s, arguing forcefully for traditional speculative rigor against the New Wave, and briefly edited Galaxy in 1977. He later wrote histories including Foundations of Science Fiction and Great Themes of Science Fiction. Darrell Schweitzer, a friend of more than 50 years, supplied the news through Pierce’s widow, Marcia; the obituary cautions that finer details remain provisional pending a formal notice. Pierce was also the son of Bell Labs engineer John R. Pierce, who coined the word “transistor,” giving his biography an unusual bridge between technological and genre history.

item.title: ICon report marks 30 years of organized Israeli science-fiction fandom
item.description: Locus published its ICon 2026 report on November 13, supplying a timely institutional snapshot in the Israeli Society for Science Fiction and Fantasy’s 30th year. The September 29–October 1 festival in Tel Aviv drew roughly 12,000 visits across three days and offered nearly 350 panels, lectures, games, workshops and performances. ICon itself is counted as either 28 or 29 years old depending on the lineage used, a familiar complication in convention history. The society, founded in May 1996, also runs conventions, reading groups, awards, grants and an online magazine. For fandom historians, the scale is noteworthy: a national fan organization created in the mid-1990s now sustains one of the field’s largest recurring volunteer-centered festivals.

item.title: Trieste festival names Species and The Squirrel among its 2026 winners
item.description: The Trieste Science+Fiction Festival announced its 26th-edition winners on November 8, 2026. Marion Le Corroller’s French-Belgian body-horror film Species (Sanguine) received the Asteroide Award for emerging genre filmmakers; the jury praised its use of horror to diagnose precarious work and a generation’s narrowing future. Markus Lehmusruusu’s Finnish-led The Squirrel won the feature Méliès d’Argent, while Alexander Peskador’s Rolling Mother took the short-film Méliès honor. The awards conclude a festival whose lineage reaches back to Trieste’s International Science Fiction Film Festival of 1963–1982. That institutional continuity, along with the Méliès network’s role in circulating European fantastic cinema, makes the results more than a routine movie-awards list.

item.title: VCON returns with a one-day ‘Pick Your Punk’ rebuilding convention
item.description: VCON 44 takes place November 14, 2026, at the BCIT Burnaby campus, marking the official return of a convention founded in 1971 and billed as Canada’s oldest fan-run speculative-fiction and games convention. The deliberately compact, one-day event is framed as a rebuilding step after the long-running three-day format went dormant. Under the theme “Pick Your Punk: Living Through the 21st Century,” programming ranges across cyberpunk, solarpunk, steampunk, hopepunk and related modes. Author Holly Schofield and artist Eric Chu are guests of honor, with William Gibson making a special appearance. The historical time peg is unusually strong: this is both VCON’s first event back and its 55th anniversary year.

item.title: Philcon prepares a 90th-anniversary gathering with a 1632 mini-convention
item.description: Philcon will mark its 90th anniversary November 20–22, 2026, in Cherry Hill, New Jersey. Founded in 1936 by the Philadelphia Science Fiction Society, it identifies itself as the world’s first and longest-running conference devoted to science fiction, fantasy and horror. This year’s principal speaker is Charlie Jane Anders, with Donato Giancola as artist guest and Sarah Pinsker as musical guest. The program also folds in a 1632 MiniCon featuring writers associated with Eric Flint’s alternate-history series, including special guest Charles Gannon. The anniversary lands squarely in fandom’s institutional history: a convention created before the first Worldcon is still using its original fan-society lineage nine decades later.

item.title: Vector opens its Modernisms issue, including a Kim Stanley Robinson interview
item.description: On November 8, 2026, the British Science Fiction Association made Vector 299, originally published in April 2024, freely available online. Guest editor Paul March-Russell assembled an issue on the contested relationship between speculative fiction and modernism, with work by Angela Acosta, Nick Hubble, Paul Kincaid, Nina Allan and Andrew M. Butler. It also includes Henry Farrell’s interview with Kim Stanley Robinson, reviews, Kat Kourbeti’s new regular column and March-Russell’s tribute to Christopher Priest. The date peg is the new open-access release, not the issue’s original publication. For researchers and fan historians, the release turns a members-only magazine issue into a durable, citable public resource.

item.title: Nalo Hopkinson receives the inaugural Andrew Pyper Prize for Genre Fiction
item.description: At the Writers’ Trust Awards on November 10, Nalo Hopkinson received the first Andrew Pyper Prize for Genre Fiction, a career award carrying C$20,000. Established after Canadian novelist Andrew Pyper’s death in 2025, the prize recognizes exceptional achievement in horror, thriller or speculative fiction and is funded for at least seven annual presentations through 2032. Hopkinson, whose work blends Caribbean folklore, science fiction and fantasy, was selected by a jury of authors and publishing professionals. The award’s launch matters beyond a single winner: it creates one of Canada’s few substantial career prizes devoted specifically to genre writing while memorializing an author associated with literary horror and thrillers.

item.title: Wisconsin’s Soulbound Books prepares a storefront devoted to science fiction and fantasy
item.description: Locus reported on November 11 that sisters Elizabeth Arpin and Katie Rittenhouse plan to open Soulbound Books in downtown Waunakee, Wisconsin. The shop will specialize in science fiction and fantasy and become the community’s only independent bookstore. Soulbound spent much of 2026 building an audience through farmers markets, library programs, brewery events and other pop-ups while work continued on its Main Street location. Its arrival is a small but meaningful publishing-infrastructure story: a physical genre bookstore is opening at a moment when many independent shops face high costs and uncertain foot traffic. The founders say their curation will range from complex space opera to cozy fantasy and romantasy, giving Madison-area readers a dedicated gathering place.

item.title: Chris Barkley and Paul Weimer join Amazing Stories to expand fandom reporting
item.description: Amazing Stories announced on November 9 that Hugo-winning fan writer Chris M. Barkley has become its lead news editor and reporter, effective November 4. Paul Weimer, a three-time Hugo-winning fan writer and podcaster, is joining the news team with him. Barkley says the expanded section will cover people, publications, conventions, awards and controversies across science fiction, fantasy and horror, with original reporting and recorded interviews. The appointments unite two writers with long records in organized fandom and signal a renewed news role for the publication that began in 1926. For File 770 readers, Weimer’s move is especially notable because it identifies a new outlet for his genre reporting and commentary.

item.title: Weird Horror ends after 13 issues as Undertow plans to close the magazine site
item.description: Undertow Publications announced on November 7 that Weird Horror has published its final issue, with Locus reporting the closure on November 9. Issue 13, released in August 2026, ends a run that began in 2020 under editor Michael Kelly. The magazine published fiction, poetry, essays and interviews; two of its stories became World Fantasy Award finalists, and others reached year’s-best anthologies and Locus recommended lists. Undertow says the economics no longer work and plans to take the Weird Horror website offline in early 2027. Print and digital copies of all 13 issues remain available for now, giving readers and bibliographers a limited window to preserve the site’s material and document a notable small-press horror venue.

item.title: Goodreads opens 2026 Choice Awards voting across five genre-heavy categories
item.description: Goodreads opened the first round of its 18th annual Choice Awards on November 10. Registered members can vote through November 22 before finalists advance to a November 24–29 round; winners will be announced December 3. The ballot places 20 nominees in each of 15 categories, including Fantasy, Romantasy, Science Fiction, Horror, and Young Adult Fantasy and Science Fiction. Goodreads says eligibility covers English-language U.S. editions, including translations and major rereleases, published from November 12, 2025, through November 10, 2026. Because nominations derive from member activity and require a 3.50 average rating at launch, the slate offers a revealing snapshot of mass-reader taste rather than a juried genre award—a distinction likely to fuel discussion about visibility, category boundaries and popularity.

item.title: SFWA sets November 15 annual business meeting with member questions to follow
item.description: The Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers Association has scheduled its annual business meeting for Sunday, November 15, 2026, at 4 p.m. Pacific. SFWA says its board, staff and selected volunteers will review the organization’s year in advocacy, education and outreach, followed by a question-and-answer session. The online meeting is a useful institutional checkpoint after a year of publishing-contract disputes, censorship fights and continuing debate over professional support for genre writers. President Kate Ristau is listed as the featured participant. For fandom and publishing observers, the immediate date peg matters: the session arrives four days after this feed update and offers members a direct opportunity to hear how SFWA frames its priorities and to press leadership on unresolved concerns.
item.source: Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers Association

item.title: M. John Harrison becomes the first established science-fiction author to win the Booker
item.description: On November 9, M. John Harrison won the 2026 Booker Prize for The End of Everything, his post-apocalyptic 13th novel. At 81 he is the prize's oldest winner, and The Guardian identified him as the first author from the established science-fiction community to take the award. The judges, chaired by Mary Beard, reached a unanimous decision and awarded Harrison £50,000. The result caps six decades of formally adventurous work spanning the Viriconium stories, the Kefahuchi Tract novels and Climbers. For genre readers, the win is both a major late-career honor and a rare moment when a central figure in British speculative fiction is recognized by one of the English-language novel's most visible institutions.

item.title: STARLOG returns to print for its 50th anniversary
item.description: STARLOG's new annual print edition reaches newsstands on November 13, almost exactly 50 years after the magazine began in 1976. The 100-page Volume 2, Issue 1 is edited by science journalist and novelist Annalee Newitz, with original reporting, artwork and conversations about science fiction and real science. STARLOG was a crucial pre-web bridge among screen fandom, convention culture and behind-the-scenes production, particularly before specialized genre coverage became ubiquitous online. Fangoria's November 3 announcement provides the immediate date peg; the revived magazine itself is the anniversary object. The return should interest readers who remember Kerry O'Quinn's original run as well as historians tracking the periodic rebirth of once-dominant fan and professional media brands.

item.title: Patrick Stewart, Star Trek's Captain Picard, dies at 86
item.description: Sir Patrick Stewart died at his Los Angeles home on October 28, his representative confirmed; CBS News updated its report on October 29. He was 86. Stewart brought Royal Shakespeare Company authority to Captain Jean-Luc Picard beginning with Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1987, then carried the role through four films and three seasons of Star Trek: Picard. He also became widely known as Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films while continuing a substantial stage career. His family's statement said he had experienced Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. The loss falls within this feed's 14-day window and marks the death of a performer whose Picard became one of modern science fiction's defining moral and intellectual figures.
